lesson_title: Selling Slices of the Business: Companies and Their Unique Transactions
hook_text: The company paid R350 000 to buy back its own shares — but only R237 500 came out of share capital. Where did the rest come from?
clip_script: Thabiso started with a spaza shop. Now he wants five more branches, and the bank will only lend so much. So he turns the business into a company and sells SLICES of it — shares. Whoever buys one owns a piece of the profits without working a single shift, and the most they can ever lose is what they paid. That promise is called limited liability, and it is the whole reason strangers fund businesses they will never manage. Now watch the transaction that trips everyone. Over the years the company sold 800 000 slices for R3 800 000 — an average of four rand seventy-five each. Then a shareholder's family wants out, and the company buys back 50 000 slices at seven rand each: R350 000. But the capital account never received seven rand for those shares — on average it received four seventy-five. So it gives back exactly what it held, R237 500, and the extra R112 500 comes out of saved-up profits: retained income. A refund of capital, plus a parting bonus paid from profits. And the bought-back slices? Torn up. Cancelled. The cake is now cut into fewer pieces — which quietly makes every remaining slice bigger.
visual_style: A growing supermarket rendered as a cake being cut into slices; share certificates flying out for rand notes flying in; at the buy-back, one payment splitting into two labelled streams — capital refund and profit bonus — before the returned slices dissolve.
pacing: Brisk story open, slow-down on the two-stream split, crisp close on the cancelled slices.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and record any share issue, buy-back, tax or dividend a paper can set.
